lead: A voltage source inverter holds the DC bus voltage steady with a capacitor and lets the load decide the current. A current source inverter does the opposite. A large series choke Ld holds the DC link current Id almost constant, and the bridge steers that current through two load lines at a time. The output current becomes a quasi-square of amplitude Id, and the load voltage is whatever the load needs. CSIs drive induction heaters, megawatt synchronous motor drives and long-cable installations. Some syllabi call this the current-fed inverter.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 and Chapter 4.2 for bridge states and 120° conduction, and see Unit 1 for reverse blocking of power devices.

sections.h3: Hold the current, not the voltage

blocks.text: In a voltage source inverter (VSI) a large capacitor sits across the DC bus. The bus voltage is stiff. When a leg switches, the load current changes only as fast as the load allows, and the bridge output is a voltage square wave.

A current source inverter (CSI) swaps the roles. A large inductor Ld in series with the DC source makes the link current stiff. The bridge connects that current to two of the three load lines at a time. The output current is a quasi-square of amplitude Id, and the load voltage is whatever the load impedance demands, v = L di/dt for an inductive load.

Ld must be large enough that Id stays nearly flat over one switching period. The link stores energy ½LdId². That energy needs a path at every instant. If a load line opens, a fuse blows or a cable falls out, the current has nowhere to go, di/dt becomes enormous and the induced voltage destroys the devices. A CSI therefore needs an overlap period between outgoing and incoming devices, or a freewheel path, or a clamp circuit.

Reverse blocking is the hard requirement. A plain IGBT blocks only a few tens of volts in reverse, so each IGBT gets a series diode. An SCR blocks reverse voltage by itself, but needs commutation, which is why SCR bridges in CSIs rely on capacitors or on the load's own EMF.

The bridge has six devices, numbered 1 to 6. With 120° conduction each device is on for 120°, so at any instant exactly two devices conduct: one from the upper group 1, 3, 5 and one from the lower group 2, 4, 6. Two load lines carry Id; the third carries nothing.

items: 0° to 60°: devices 6 and 1 conduct; current enters line A and returns through line B.
60° to 120°: devices 1 and 2; line A in, line C out.
120° to 180°: devices 2 and 3; line B in, line C out.
180° to 240°: devices 3 and 4; line B in, line A out.
240° to 300°: devices 4 and 5; line C in, line A out.
300° to 360°: devices 5 and 6; line C in, line B out.

blocks.text: Each line current is therefore +Id for 120°, zero for 60°, −Id for 120°, zero for 60°.

blocks.where: I₁ is the rms value of the fundamental line current; I(rms) is the rms value of the whole quasi-square line current; Id is the DC link current in amperes.

blocks.text: The waveform has no triplen harmonics because the load is three-wire. The 5th harmonic is 20% of the fundamental, the 7th is 14.3%, the 11th is 9.1% and the 13th is 7.7%, which gives a current total harmonic distortion near 31%.

The load voltage is not square. With a motor load, leakage inductance and any parallel capacitor smooth the current pulses into a nearly sinusoidal voltage. In a star load the line current equals the phase current; in delta the phase current is the line current divided by √3.

sections.h3: Where CSIs are used, and how they fail

blocks.text: Medium-voltage, high-power drives are the main home. A load-commutated inverter (LCI) uses SCRs and takes its commutation voltage from the motor's own back EMF. Such drives run synchronous motors of several megawatts in pumps, fans and compressors.

Induction heating is a natural fit. The work coil and a parallel capacitor form a tank circuit that wants a sinusoidal voltage. Feeding it from a current source lets the capacitor absorb the current harmonics while the tank rings at resonance (see Unit 6, Induction heating).

Long cables favour the CSI too. A VSI sending fast voltage edges down a long feeder suffers charging current and reflected waves. A CSI at the sending end, with a capacitor at the load end, behaves better.

Four weak points to remember. An open load is destructive. An LCI cannot start at standstill, because a stopped motor has no EMF to turn the SCRs off. Series diodes add conduction loss when IGBTs are used. On the plus side, regeneration is easy: reverse the DC link voltage with a dual converter at the supply side while Id keeps its direction.

figure.caption: The choke fixes the link current Id and the bridge steers it through two load lines at a time, so the load receives a current quasi-square rather than a voltage square wave.

spec.title: Current source inverter
spec.aria: A DC source feeds a large series choke that fixes the current, and a bridge with reverse-blocking devices steers that current into the load.

examples.question: A three-phase current source inverter has a DC link current Id = 50 A and uses 120° conduction. It feeds a star-connected resistive load of 2 Ω per phase. Find (a) the rms fundamental line current, (b) the total rms line current, (c) the fundamental power delivered to the load, and (d) the rms harmonic current and the current THD.
steps: Step 1. The line current is a quasi-square of amplitude Id = 50 A, on for 120° and zero for 60° in each half cycle. Its fundamental rms is I₁ = (√6/π)Id = (2.4495/3.1416)×50 = 0.7797×50 = 38.98 A.
Step 2. The total rms of the same wave is I = Id√(2/3) = 50×0.8165 = 40.82 A.
Step 3. The load is star, so line current equals phase current. The fundamental phase voltage is V₁ = I₁R = 38.98×2 = 77.97 V.
Step 4. Fundamental power P₁ = 3I₁²R = 3×(38.98)²×2 = 3×1519.8×2 = 9118.9 W, about 9.12 kW.
examples.answer: I₁ = 38.98 A (about 39 A), total rms 40.82 A, fundamental power 9.12 kW, harmonic current 12.12 A and current THD 31.1%.
examples.check:
import math
Id = 50.0
R = 2.0
I1 = math.sqrt(6)/math.pi*Id
Irms = Id*math.sqrt(2/3)
P1 = 3*I1**2*R
Ih = math.sqrt(Irms**2 - I1**2)
thd = Ih/I1*100
print(round(I1,2))
print(round(Irms,2))
print(round(P1,1))
print(round(Ih,2))
print(round(thd,1))

traps: Using Id directly as the rms output current. Id is the peak of the quasi-square; the fundamental rms is 0.78 Id and the total rms is 0.816 Id.
Forgetting the series diode. A plain IGBT cannot block reverse voltage, and the load voltage does reverse in a CSI, so every IGBT needs one.
Expecting a square output voltage. The CSI fixes the current; the voltage follows the load impedance, and with a motor plus capacitor it comes out close to a sine.
Ignoring the open-circuit danger. Breaking the load current with a large choke produces a destructive voltage spike; a real CSI needs overlap, a freewheel path or a clamp.
Confusing a CSI with the current-controlled VSI of Chapter 4.9. A grid-tied inverter controls its current by PWM, but its DC link is still a capacitor, so it is a VSI.

quiz.q: What element makes the DC link of a CSI stiff, and what quantity does it hold constant?
quiz.a: A large series inductor Ld in the DC link; it holds the link current Id constant.

quiz.q: Why does each IGBT in a CSI need a diode in series with it?
quiz.a: The load voltage reverses every half cycle, so an off device can be reverse-biased. An IGBT has almost no reverse blocking capability; the series diode supplies it. An SCR would not need one because it blocks reverse voltage itself.

quiz.q: A three-phase CSI with 120° conduction has Id = 80 A. Find the fundamental rms line current and the total rms line current.
A CSI with Id = 100 A feeds a delta-connected load of 5 Ω per phase. Find the fundamental power delivered.
A CSI feeds an induction motor with a capacitor across its terminals. Explain why the current is a quasi-square but the voltage is nearly sinusoidal.
quiz.a: The bridge forces Id as a quasi-square current into the motor-capacitor combination. The capacitor presents a low impedance to the 5th, 7th and higher current harmonics and absorbs them, while the fundamental flows into the motor. The terminal voltage is the capacitor voltage, so it is nearly sinusoidal. The harmonic currents circulate in the capacitor and raise its rating.

quiz.q: An LCI driving a synchronous motor cannot start it from standstill. Why, and what is done?
quiz.a: Load commutation needs the motor's back EMF to reverse-bias the conducting SCR. At standstill there is no EMF, so the SCR cannot be turned off. The drive is started with forced commutation, with a separate starting arrangement, or the motor is run up on a VSI or a DC machine before handover.

quiz.q: State two differences between a VSI and a CSI.
quiz.a: The VSI has a capacitor that fixes the DC voltage and its output is a voltage square wave; the CSI has an inductor that fixes the DC current and its output is a current quasi-square. The VSI switch needs only forward blocking with a freewheel diode; the CSI switch needs reverse blocking, usually a series diode.

quiz.q: Write the formula for the fundamental rms line current of a three-phase CSI with 120° conduction.
quiz.a: I₁ = (√6/π) Id ≈ 0.78 Id, where Id is the DC link current.

beyond: Not for the exam. Medium-voltage drives above a few megawatts increasingly use PWM current-source converters with IGCTs or reverse-blocking IGBTs, because the DC choke survives a short circuit and the output capacitor gives a clean voltage. Current-source converters are also studied for offshore HVDC links and for grid-forming inverters that must limit fault current rather than trip. Wide-bandgap SiC devices with true reverse blocking would remove the series diode. Search for load-commutated inverter, PWM current source rectifier and reverse-blocking IGCT.
